text.en: Every apple on your plate, every book in your bag and every tonne of coal in a power plant has travelled. Transport is called the lifeline of a country because it carries people and goods from where they are to where they are needed. Let us study India's land, water and air transport one by one.

Transport is the system by which passengers and goods are carried from one place to another, and it is called the lifeline of a country.
Early people travelled on foot or with animals, and the discovery of the wheel made transport easier, until we got three major means: land, water and air.
Roadways carry goods and passengers over short, medium and long distances, and they are cheap to build and maintain, so they are the most universal mode of transport.
The densest road network is in the northern plains, the highest road density is in Kerala and the lowest in Jammu and Kashmir.
Shershah Suri built the Shahi road from the Indus valley to the Sonar valley in Bengal, which the British renamed the Grand Trunk Road, and today it runs from Amritsar to Kolkata.
For construction and maintenance, roads are classified as national highways, state highways, district roads, rural roads, border roads and international highways.
National highways link state capitals, major ports, rail junctions and industrial and tourist centres, and they are developed by the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways.
The longest national highway is NH-44 from Srinagar to Kanniyakumari covering 4,112 km, and the shortest is NH-47A from Kundanoor to Kochi port covering only 6 km.
The National Highways Authority of India, NHAI, was established in 1995 as an autonomous body under the Ministry of Surface Transport.
State highways link important cities, towns and district headquarters within a state and are built by the state governments, while district roads connect district and taluk headquarters and are built by the Public Works Department.
Rural roads connect villages to nearby towns and are maintained by village panchayats, while border roads of strategic value are built by the Border Roads Organisation set up in 1960.
The Border Roads Organisation built the world's highest road joining Chandigarh and Leh at an average height of 4,270 metres.
The Golden Quadrilateral is a 5,846 km long road of four to six lanes joining Delhi, Kolkata, Chennai and Mumbai, launched in 1999.
The North-South corridor joins Srinagar and Kanniyakumari with 4,076 km, the East-West corridor joins Silchar and Porbandar with 3,640 km, and they cross at Jhansi.
Expressways are multi-lane high-speed roads such as Mumbai-Pune and Yamuna between Delhi and Agra, and international highways link India to Pakistan, Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh and Myanmar.
Railways are the backbone of India's surface transport, carry bulky goods and large numbers of passengers, and help in the commercialisation of agriculture and national integration.
The Indian Railway network is the fourth largest in the world and is organised into 17 zones, for example Southern Railway at Chennai and Konkan Railway at Navi Mumbai.
By the width of the track there are four gauges: broad gauge 1.676 m, metre gauge 1 m, narrow gauge 0.762 m and light gauge 0.610 m.
The first suburban railway started in Mumbai in 1925, and the Gatiman Express between New Delhi and Agra, touching 160 km per hour, is the fastest train.
Eight cities have metro rail, namely Kolkata, Chennai, Delhi, Bengaluru, Gurgaon, Mumbai, Jaipur and Kochi, and the Kolkata metro was the first.
Pipelines carry oil, natural gas and even solids as slurry, and their first cost is high but the running cost is very low, as in the lines from Upper Assam to Kanpur and Hazira to Jagdishpur.
Waterways are the oldest and cheapest transport, fuel-efficient and eco-friendly, and are of two types: inland waterways and ocean routes.
The Inland Waterways Authority was set up in 1986, National Waterway 1 runs from Haldia to Allahabad for 1,620 km, National Waterway 2 on the Brahmaputra from Dhubri to Sadiya for 891 km and National Waterway 3 from Kollam to Kottapuram for 205 km.
About 95 percent of India's foreign trade by volume and 70 percent by value moves by ocean routes through 13 major and about 200 minor ports.
The east coast major ports are Kolkata, Paradip, Visakhapatnam, Chennai, Ennore and Tuticorin, and the west coast ports are Kandla, Mumbai, Nhava Sheva, New Mangalore, Marmagao and Kochi.
India's four major shipyards are at Visakhapatnam, Kolkata (Garden Reach), Mumbai (Mazagaon) and Kochi.
Air transport is the quickest and costliest mode, it reaches mountains and deserts, and it is vital in floods, epidemics and wars.
Air transport began in India on 18 February 1918 when Henry Piquet carried mail from Allahabad to Naini, the airlines were nationalised in 1953, and the Airports Authority of India was formed in 1995.
Indian Airlines served domestic routes and Air India served international routes, there are 19 designated international airports, and Pavan Hans gives helicopter service to the petroleum sector and the northeast.

problem.en: A train must carry coal for 600 km, a distance where the fuel cost per tonne is 3 rupees per km by road and 1 rupee per km by rail. Compare the costs for 100 tonnes.

text.en: Road cost is 100 x 600 x 3 = 1,80,000 rupees.
Rail cost is 100 x 600 x 1 = 60,000 rupees.

why.en: Same method with the rail rate.

text.en: Rail saves 1,20,000 rupees, which is why bulky goods such as coal go by rail.

why.en: Railways are best for bulky goods over long distances.

prompt.en: Explain why roads are called the most universal mode of transport and why waterways are the cheapest, with one example of each from India.

requiredIdeas.en: Roads are cheap to build and reach every village, for example rural roads linked by panchayats
Waterways are the oldest and cheapest and carry heavy bulky goods, for example about 95 percent of foreign trade goes by sea
Air transport is quickest but costliest and is useful in remote areas

commonMisconceptions.en: The Golden Quadrilateral joins Delhi Kolkata Chennai and Bengaluru (it joins Delhi, Kolkata, Chennai and Mumbai)
Broad gauge is 1 metre wide (it is 1.676 metres)

points.en: Land transport: roads, railways, pipelines. Water: inland and ocean. Air: domestic and international.
NH-44 is the longest highway (4,112 km), the Golden Quadrilateral links four metros (5,846 km).
Railways have 17 zones and four gauges, with the broad gauge 1.676 m.
About 95% of foreign trade goes by sea through 13 major ports, and air transport began in 1918.
